hints: Look carefully at the connectivity first. Do the two molecules have the same carbon skeleton and the same positions for the double bonds and the OH group?
Now zoom in on the C=C bond next to the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group. Notice how the $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ swap sides between geraniol and nerol.
Remember that restricted rotation about a C=C with two different groups on each carbon allows two different spatial arrangements. Think which name we give to that cis-trans type relationship.
walkthrough:
**Check the skeleton and functional groups**

Both molecules have the same long carbon chain, the same two C=C double bonds in the same places, and the same $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ alcohol group at the end. So nothing has moved to a new position.

Connectivity is identical: $$\text{same molecular formula, same skeleton}$$

**Focus on the key C=C bond**

Look at the right-hand double bond, $\text{C}=\text{C}(\text{H})(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})$. Each carbon of this double bond has two different groups attached, and rotation is restricted.

Left C has: $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2...$
Right C has: $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$

**Compare the spatial arrangement**

In geraniol, the two larger carbon groups are on opposite sides of the double bond (trans / E arrangement). In nerol, they are on the same side (cis / Z arrangement).

This difference in space around a C=C with no change in connectivity is exactly: $$\text{geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism}$$

options.A: Chain isomerism needs a different arrangement of the carbon skeleton, for example straight chain versus branched. Here both molecules have the identical branched 10-carbon skeleton, so this is not chain isomerism.
options.B: Correct. The connectivity is the same but the groups around the C=C bond next to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ are arranged differently in space. Geraniol is the trans (E) form and nerol is the cis (Z) form, which is classic geometrical isomerism.
options.C: Optical isomerism needs a chiral centre, a carbon with four different groups, giving non-superimposable mirror images. Neither molecule has a chiral centre and the two structures are not mirror images, they differ only at one C=C.
options.D: Positional isomerism needs the same skeleton but the functional group or multiple bond in a different position, for example OH on carbon 1 versus carbon 2. Here the OH and both double bonds are in exactly the same positions, only their 3D orientation differs.
